context.concept_name: Measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode)

coverage.learning_objective: Compute the mean, median, and mode of a dataset and choose which one best represents its typical (central) value, especially when the data is skewed.

required_facts.statement: The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations.
The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values.
The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a batch of seven delivery orders whose delivery times, in minutes, are 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, and 80. Before you can say anything useful about this batch, you need one number that answers "what's typical here?" -- and there are three different ways to compute that number.

The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations. For the seven delivery times, the sum is 18+20+22+22+26+28+80 = 216, and 216 divided by 7 is about 30.9 minutes.

The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values. Sorted, the seven times are 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 -- the middle (fourth) value is 22 minutes.
The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode. In this batch, 22 minutes appears twice while every other value appears once, so 22 is the mode.

Notice that the mean (about 30.9 minutes) sits well above the median and mode (both 22 minutes). That gap exists because the mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset. Here, the single 80-minute delivery pulls the mean upward far more than it moves the median, so 22 minutes -- not 30.9 -- is the more representative "typical" delivery time for this batch.

Mean, median, and mode all try to answer "what's typical," but they compute it differently, and the mean and median react differently to a batch that includes one unusually large value -- so before reporting a single center number, it's worth checking whether an extreme value like that 80-minute delivery is pulling the mean away from where most of the data actually sits.

video_need.reason: Sorting the values and locating the middle position, or watching the mean shift as the 80-minute delivery is added or removed, would reinforce the sensitivity comparison, but the worked calculation above already walks through the sum, the sort, and the count-based reasoning step by step.

practice_anchor.objective: Given seven delivery times with one unusually large value, compute the mean, median and mode, then say which best represents a typical delivery time and why.
practice_anchor.success: The learner sums and divides for the mean, finds the middle value of the sorted list for the median, names the most frequent value as the mode, and picks the median because the large value pulls the mean up.

visual_anchor.purpose: A sorted row of delivery times with the mean, median and mode marked, so the large value visibly pulls the mean away from the median.

teaching_notes: The dataset (18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 minutes) is reused across measures of center and spread for continuity -- keep the sum (216), mean (~30.9), median (22), and mode (22) consistent everywhere they reappear.

The word 'skewed' above is used only in the informal sense the brief's own fact (f4) already uses it in, not as a defined term.

context.concept_name: Measures of spread (range, variance, standard deviation)

coverage.learning_objective: Compute the range, variance, and standard deviation of a dataset and interpret what each says about how spread out the data are.

required_facts.statement: The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value.

The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean.

The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread.

teaching_blocks.content: Knowing the typical delivery time (22 minutes, from the median) doesn't say how spread out the batch is. Most of the seven delivery times (18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 minutes) cluster fairly close together, but one sits far away -- spread measures capture that difference.
The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value. For this batch, that's 80 minus 18, or 62 minutes.

The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean. With a mean of about 30.9 minutes, the seven squared deviations sum to about 2886.9, and dividing by n - 1 = 6 gives a variance of about 481.1 (in minutes squared).

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean. The square root of about 481.1 is about 21.9 minutes -- roughly how far a typical delivery time sits from the 30.9-minute mean.

The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread. That's why "about 21.9 minutes" (the standard deviation) is easier to interpret directly than "about 481.1 minutes squared" (the variance) -- and why the range (62 minutes) says nothing about whether the other five delivery times are bunched tightly or scattered widely.

Range, variance, and standard deviation all quantify spread, but the range only looks at the two extremes, while variance and standard deviation take every observation's distance from the mean into account -- with standard deviation, unlike variance, expressed in the original units, and so usually the easiest to talk about in context.

video_need.reason: Watching each deviation get squared and visualized as a bar, or seeing a number line with the mean and spread marked, would build intuition for 'average squared distance,' but the worked variance-then-standard-deviation calculation above already walks through every step of the computation.

segments.label: Variance and standard deviation worked from squared deviations, for a whole population and then for a sample
segments.summary: Works through variance and standard deviation on a small set of measurements. Squaring makes the units squared, so the square root is taken to get a standard deviation of 10 in the original units, drawn as the mean plus and minus that distance. The clip then explains that real data is usually a sample, so the sample mean is used and the total is divided by one less than the number of values, because dividing by the full count would consistently underestimate the spread. context.concept_name: Basic A/B test structure (control vs treatment group)

coverage.learning_objective: Given a description of an experiment, identify its control group, its treatment group, and the metric being compared between them.

required_facts.statement: Studies where researchers assign treatments to cases are called experiments; when the assignment includes randomization, it is called a randomized experiment.
Researchers randomly assign cases to a control group and a treatment group so that differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled are evened out.

A/B testing works by showing two variants of a page or experience to users at random: the original (control, or A) and a modified version (variation, or B); engagement with each version is measured and then compared against the baseline, the control.

teaching_blocks.content: The delivery company wants to know whether a redesigned checkout button on its ordering app gets more people to complete an order. Rather than guess, it runs a controlled test on real users.

Studies where researchers assign treatments to cases are called experiments; when the assignment includes randomization, it is called a randomized experiment. Researchers randomly assign cases to a control group and a treatment group so that differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled are evened out.

A/B testing works by showing two variants of a page or experience to users at random: the original (control, or A) and a modified version (variation, or B); engagement with each version is measured and then compared against the baseline, the control. For the checkout button, the existing button is the control (A), the redesigned button is the treatment (B), users are randomly shown one or the other, and the metric compared is the share of each group that completes an order.
Every A/B test has these parts: a control group, a treatment group, and the measure being compared between them. The treatment group's result is then compared against the control, the baseline.

video_need.reason: Randomly splitting one population of users into two groups that each experience something different is a spatial/process relationship -- a diagram showing users being randomly routed into a control arm and a treatment arm makes the structure clearer than describing the split in words.

media.group_title: A/B test structure: two variants, one metric, one baseline

segments.label: Defining A/B test structure: control group, treatment group, and the metric tracked
segments.summary: A/B testing (also called split testing) grew out of randomized controlled trials. The core idea: show the new or varied version of a product to one sample of users — the experimental group — and the existing version to a separate sample — the control group. The difference in product performance between the two groups is then tracked over the test period. If the varied version underperforms, the business can decide whether to refine it or explore other directions.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the clip names the two groups and what gets measured. Note: the clip calls the treatment group the 'experimental group' — Devspace uses 'treatment group'.
bridge_note.after: The clip covers f3's structure but does not explain randomized assignment (f1, f2). The teaching text covers both.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a short description of an A/B test scenario, identify which group is the control, which is the treatment, and which metric is being compared between them.
practice_anchor.success: The learner correctly labels the control group (original/A), the treatment group (modified/B), and names the single metric used to compare the two groups, with no confusion between the two roles.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a population of users being randomly split into two arms — a control arm (original experience, A) and a treatment arm (modified experience, B) — with a metric arrow pointing from each arm to a comparison step, making the structure and the direction of comparison visible at a glance.

coverage.learning_objective: Compute and interpret the lift (percentage change) between a treatment group's result and a control group's result.

required_facts.statement: Relative improvement (lift) is the percentage difference in the variation's conversion rate over the baseline (control) conversion rate; for example, a 10% relative improvement over a 25% baseline conversion rate means the variation's conversion rate is 27.5%.
Relative improvement describes the variation's change as a percentage of the baseline's rate.
Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control).

teaching_blocks.content: Once the checkout-button test has run, the raw numbers -- say, a 20% completion rate for the control button and a 22% completion rate for the redesigned one -- need to be turned into a comparison that's easy to talk about.

Relative improvement (lift) is the percentage difference in the variation's conversion rate over the baseline (control) conversion rate; for example, a 10% relative improvement over a 25% baseline conversion rate means the variation's conversion rate is 27.5%. Relative improvement describes the variation's change as a percentage of the baseline's rate.

Applying that to the checkout test: a treatment rate of 22% over a control rate of 20% is a 2-percentage-point difference, which as a percentage of the 20% baseline is a 10% lift -- the same 10%-relative-improvement structure as the textbook example, just with the checkout numbers.

Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control). Lift puts the observed difference into one figure: a positive lift means the variation's rate came out above the control's in this test, and a negative lift means it came out below.

video_need.reason: Lift is a percentage-change calculation on two numbers that are already known; the worked example fully shows how to compute and read it, with no mechanism, UI, or changing state to demonstrate.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a control conversion rate and a treatment conversion rate as Python floats, write a function that computes the lift and returns a string stating whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect and by how much.
practice_anchor.success: The function correctly computes lift as (treatment - control) / control * 100, returns a string that includes the numeric lift value and correctly labels the direction (positive, negative, or neutral) for at least three distinct input pairs.

live_code.required_skill: Define a function that accepts two float arguments, performs arithmetic to compute percentage change, uses a conditional to classify the result, and returns a formatted string.

context.concept_name: Integrating SQL querying into an end-to-end project

coverage.learning_objective: Combine already-learned SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, and GROUP BY into one SQL query that retrieves the specific rows, columns, and groups the capstone's business question needs.

required_facts.statement: A single SELECT statement's syntax allows a FROM clause, a WHERE clause, and a GROUP BY clause to appear together in the same query.

A join, such as an INNER JOIN, can be included in that same SELECT statement's FROM clause to combine matching rows from more than one table before the query's WHERE filtering or GROUP BY grouping is applied.

teaching_blocks.content: The first executable step of the workflow is retrieving last quarter's orders with SQL.

A single SELECT statement's syntax allows a FROM clause, a WHERE clause, and a GROUP BY clause to appear together in the same query. In the capstone, that means the orders query can filter down to last quarter's rows and group the result by zone in one statement, rather than as separate steps.

A join, such as an INNER JOIN, can be included in that same SELECT statement's FROM clause to combine matching rows from more than one table before the query's WHERE filtering or GROUP BY grouping is applied. In the capstone, that means the orders and drivers tables can be joined in the same FROM clause, before the WHERE and GROUP BY narrow and group the combined rows.

Combined, the capstone's retrieval query looks like: SELECT o.zone, AVG(o.delivery_time) FROM orders o INNER JOIN drivers d ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-04-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-07-01' GROUP BY o.zone; -- the join combines each order with its matching driver row first, the WHERE clause then narrows the rows to last quarter (April 1 to June 30), and the GROUP BY groups what's left by zone, so AVG gives one average delivery time per zone.
None of this is new SQL syntax -- it's the same SELECT, FROM, WHERE, JOIN, and GROUP BY already learned, aimed at the capstone's own question.

video_need.reason: Watching the joined, filtered, grouped query actually run and return zone-level rows helps confirm the clause ordering, though the text's worked query already shows the full combination.

context.concept_name: Integrating spreadsheet analysis into an end-to-end project

coverage.learning_objective: Apply already-learned spreadsheet formulas and PivotTables to complete the capstone project's spreadsheet-based analysis step.

required_facts.statement: A PivotTable is built by selecting the data range and inserting a PivotTable, then adding fields to it: non-numeric fields default to Rows, date/time fields to Columns, and numeric fields to Values, and fields can be dragged between these areas to rearrange the summary.
COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2]…) applies criteria across one or more ranges and counts the cells for which all the criteria are met.

teaching_blocks.content: For part of the analysis, the driver roster's shift and zone details are paired with each order's delivery_time in one sheet, so that step runs in spreadsheet tools instead of SQL.

A PivotTable is built by selecting the data range and inserting a PivotTable, then adding fields to it: non-numeric fields default to Rows, date/time fields to Columns, and numeric fields to Values, and fields can be dragged between these areas to rearrange the summary. In the capstone, that means the delivery sheet's zone and shift fields default into Rows while delivery_time defaults into Values, ready to be rearranged into a more useful layout.

COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2]...) applies criteria across one or more ranges and counts the cells for which all the criteria are met. In the capstone, that means counting how many deliveries in a specific zone exceeded a time threshold, using the zone and the time as the two criteria.

For the capstone's delivery sheet, where each row pairs an order's zone and delivery_time with its driver's shift from the roster: selecting the data range, inserting a PivotTable and adding those fields puts zone and shift -- both non-numeric -- in Rows by default, and delivery_time, which is numeric, in Values. Dragging shift from Rows to Columns rearranges the summary into a zone-by-shift grid, and changing the Values field's summary function to Average makes each cell an average delivery time. Separately, COUNTIFS(zone_range, "Ikeja", delivery_time_range, ">45") counts how many Ikeja deliveries in the sheet took more than 45 minutes, since both criteria -- the zone and the time threshold -- must be met at once.
The PivotTable and COUNTIFS skills already learned are now run on this project's own roster and delivery data instead of a practice file.

context.concept_name: Integrating Python/pandas cleaning and analysis into an end-to-end project

coverage.learning_objective: Apply already-learned pandas cleaning (isna/dropna/fillna) and analysis (groupby aggregation) to the capstone's own retrieved dataset.

required_facts.statement: isna() detects which values in a DataFrame are missing, and dropna() removes rows with missing values or fillna() replaces them with a specified value.

A groupby operation splits data into groups based on some criteria, applies a function independently to each group, and combines the results back into a single structure; an aggregation is a groupby operation that reduces each group to one summary value per column.

teaching_blocks.content: Once orders and roster are both retrieved, pandas is where they get cleaned and combined for the actual analysis.

isna() detects which values in a DataFrame are missing, and dropna() removes rows with missing values or fillna() replaces them with a specified value. In the capstone, that means flagging which of the retrieved orders are missing a delivery_time before deciding whether to drop or fill those rows.

A groupby operation splits data into groups based on some criteria, applies a function independently to each group, and combines the results back into a single structure; an aggregation is a groupby operation that reduces each group to one summary value per column. In the capstone, that means splitting the cleaned orders by zone and reducing each zone's delivery times to one summary number.

On the capstone's retrieved orders, orders['delivery_time'].isna() flags rows with no delivery time recorded; those rows get removed with dropna() (or, where a default makes sense, filled with fillna()). Then orders.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean() splits the cleaned orders by zone, computes the mean delivery time independently within each zone, and combines the per-zone results into one summary -- an aggregation, since each zone group is reduced to a single number.
The same isna()/dropna()/fillna() and groupby skills already learned are now run on the capstone's own retrieved data instead of a practice dataset.

context.concept_name: Building a data model for the capstone dataset

coverage.learning_objective: Connect the capstone project's own tables using the correct primary keys, foreign keys, and one-to-many relationships.

required_facts.statement: A primary key uniquely identifies each row of a table; a foreign key's values must match values appearing in some row of the table it references.

In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side (for example, one department has many employees); in the Customer/Order example, the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table.

teaching_blocks.content: The capstone's data spans two tables -- Orders and Drivers -- so before deeper analysis relies on both together, they need to be modeled as related tables.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row of a table; a foreign key's values must match values appearing in some row of the table it references. In the capstone, that means the Drivers table needs a column that uniquely identifies each driver, and the Orders table needs a column whose values must match one of those driver identifiers.

In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side (for example, one department has many employees); in the Customer/Order example, the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table. In the capstone, that means one driver can appear in many orders, the same one-to-many pattern as one customer having many orders.

Mapped onto the capstone: Drivers has driver_id as its primary key, uniquely identifying each driver row. Orders has its own primary key, order_id, plus a driver_id column that is a foreign key -- its values must match a driver_id that already exists in Drivers. Since one driver delivers many orders, this is a one-to-many relationship: one row on the Drivers ('one') side relates to many rows on the Orders ('many') side, the same pattern as CustID sitting in the Order table and matching a valid CustID in the Customer table.
Getting the primary key/foreign key pairing right connects the two tables correctly before any join or aggregation across them can be trusted.

coverage.learning_objective: Compute and interpret the descriptive statistics (using pandas) that support the capstone project's business question.

required_facts.statement: describe() computes a variety of summary statistics about a Series or the columns of a DataFrame.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations than the median, which is more robust to them; so when the goal is to understand a typical individual value in a skewed dataset, the median can be more useful.

teaching_blocks.content: With cleaned, modeled data, the business question needs actual numbers: how late are deliveries, by zone?

describe() computes a variety of summary statistics about a Series or the columns of a DataFrame. In the capstone, that means running describe() on a zone's delivery_time column to get that summary in one call.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations than the median, which is more robust to them; so when the goal is to understand a typical individual value in a skewed dataset, the median can be more useful. In the capstone, that means checking whether a handful of unusually long deliveries are skewing a zone's average before trusting it as typical.

Running describe() on one zone's delivery_time column returns a mean of 52 minutes, with the median (the middle quartile in describe()'s output) at 38 minutes. But a handful of deliveries in that zone took over three hours -- a stalled vehicle, a wrong address -- and the mean is pulled up by those extreme observations, while the median, more robust to them, stays at 38 minutes. The capstone's business question is which zones are missing the delivery-time target and by how much, which calls for judging a typical delivery against that target rather than one skewed by a few rare extremes, so the median is the more useful number here.
describe() gives the full summary; deciding whether the mean or the median actually answers the business question depends on whether extreme values are skewing that particular column.

video_need.reason: describe()'s output is a static table, and the mean-vs-median contrast is a numeric comparison the worked example already spells out; a simple table view is enough on top of that.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a DataFrame containing a delivery_time column for a single zone, call describe() on that column, then compare the mean and median values it returns and state in a comment which statistic better represents a typical delivery for a skewed distribution.
practice_anchor.success: describe() is called on the delivery_time column; the learner reads the mean and median from the output; a comment identifies the median as the more useful measure and explains that extreme values pull the mean upward.

live_code.required_skill: Call describe() on a pandas Series and read mean and median from its output; reason about which central-tendency measure is appropriate given skew.
live_code.starter_state_intent: A small DataFrame named df is pre-loaded with a delivery_time column for one zone; the column contains a few extreme high values so that mean and median differ visibly.
live_code.observable_success: describe() output is produced; the learner's comment correctly identifies the median as the better measure of a typical delivery and references the influence of extreme observations on the mean.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the describe() output table for a delivery_time column where the mean (e.g. 52 min) is noticeably higher than the median (e.g. 38 min), making the skew-driven divergence between the two statistics immediately visible.

teaching_notes: Applies already-learned describe() and mean/median robustness to the capstone's own delivery_time column -- keep the statistics themselves brief, the point is which one answers this question.

context.concept_name: Building a polished matplotlib/seaborn visualization set for the capstone

coverage.learning_objective: Build a coherent set of matplotlib/seaborn charts, arranged and annotated, that presents the capstone's key findings to a stakeholder audience.

required_facts.statement: fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2) creates one Figure containing a 2x2 grid of Axes, so several charts can share one figure.
plt.subplot(131), plt.subplot(132), and plt.subplot(133) can each hold a different chart side by side in one figure, and plt.suptitle() adds one title over the whole figure.

teaching_blocks.content: The findings now need a visualization set a stakeholder can look at, not just numbers in a table.

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2) creates one Figure containing a 2x2 grid of Axes, so several charts can share one figure. In the capstone, that means four related delivery charts can share one figure instead of as four separate figures.

plt.subplot(131), plt.subplot(132), and plt.subplot(133) can each hold a different chart side by side in one figure, and plt.suptitle() adds one title over the whole figure. In the capstone, that means three of the delivery charts can instead sit side by side under one shared title.

For the capstone, fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2) lays out four related charts -- delivery time by zone, delivery time by shift, order count by zone, and the distribution of delivery times -- in one 2x2 figure. Alternatively, plt.subplot(131), plt.subplot(132), plt.subplot(133) place three of those charts side by side in a single row, and plt.suptitle('Delivery Performance -- Last Quarter') puts one title over all three so they read as one visualization set.
Either layout turns several separate charts into one coherent figure the stakeholder summary can point to as a set.

video_need.reason: Building a multi-panel figure and watching how subplots(2,2) or side-by-side subplot() calls arrange on screen is a spatial layout task that a live demo shows far better than a description.

media.group_title: Arranging multiple charts in one figure with subplots

segments.label: plt.subplots(2, 2) — one figure, four axes
segments.summary: The instructor defines a figure as the overall canvas and an axes object as a single plot within it. Calling plt.subplots(2, 2) returns a figure and a 2-D array of four axes objects. Each axes is then addressed by its row and column index — axs[0,0], axs[0,1], axs[1,0], axs[1,1] — and plotted independently with its own data, color, and title. plt.tight_layout() is called to prevent the four panels from overlapping. The demo uses simple power-of-x curves rather than a stakeholder dataset, but the layout mechanics are identical to what the capstone requires.

bridge_note.before: Watch how each axes is addressed by [row, col] index and given its own title. Note: the clip uses toy curves, not delivery data, and does not cover plt.subplot(131)/plt.suptitle().
bridge_note.after: The clip shows f1 in action. The text covers f2 — the side-by-side plt.subplot(131/132/133) pattern and plt.suptitle() — which this clip omits entirely.

practice_anchor.objective: Using the capstone delivery dataset, build a multi-panel figure that places at least three related charts together in one figure and adds a single shared title over all panels.
practice_anchor.success: Running the cell produces one figure containing multiple axes, each with its own chart and individual title, and a shared figure-level title produced by plt.suptitle(); no separate plt.show() calls are needed per chart.

live_code.required_skill: Arrange multiple matplotlib axes inside a single figure using either plt.subplots(2, 2) or plt.subplot(1, 3, n) calls, and add a shared title with plt.suptitle().
live_code.starter_state_intent: A DataFrame named df is already loaded with columns: zone (str), shift (str), delivery_time_min (float), order_count (int). No figure or axes objects exist yet.
live_code.observable_success: A single figure appears containing either a 2x2 grid or a 1x3 row of charts; each panel has an individual title; plt.suptitle() text is visible above all panels; no IndexError or AxesSubplot shape mismatch is raised.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the two multi-panel patterns side by side — the plt.subplots(2, 2) / axs[row, col] pattern and the plt.subplot(131)/plt.subplot(132)/plt.subplot(133)/plt.suptitle() pattern — so learners can see the structural difference before writing their own capstone figure.

teaching_notes: This applies already-learned matplotlib plotting to the capstone's own figures -- don't re-teach individual chart types, only the multi-panel arrangement.

clusters.title: Measures of Center and Spread
clusters.reasoning: Measures of center (mean, median, mode) and measures of spread (variance, standard deviation, IQR) are the two complementary halves of descriptive statistics — they answer 'where is the data?' and 'how spread out is it?' respectively. They are always interpreted together and form one idea: summarizing a distribution numerically.

clusters.title: A/B Test Structure and Lift
clusters.reasoning: A/B test structure (control vs treatment, random assignment, metric selection) and lift interpretation (the relative improvement of treatment over control) are two aspects of the same experiment: how to design it and how to read its primary result. A learner cannot interpret lift without understanding the test structure that produced it.

clusters.title: Integrating SQL, Spreadsheets, and pandas
clusters.reasoning: Integrating SQL, spreadsheets, and pandas are three parallel tool-application steps in the capstone workflow — each applies one of the path's core tools to the project dataset. They read as variants of one idea: using each tool for what it does best in a real analysis. Building the data model is a structural design task that precedes or accompanies tool integration and is better shown separately.

clusters.title: Applying Statistics and Building the Visualization
clusters.reasoning: Applying descriptive statistics and building the dashboard or visualization set are two sequential steps of the capstone's analysis and presentation phase: compute the summaries, then visualize them. The statistics inform what to show; the visualization makes it communicable. They read as two parts of one idea: turning data into insight.
